title: Our Course Materials Have a New Audience
author: Marc Watkins
summary: Marc Watkins argues that higher education should stop circling academic-integrity questions about AI and instead help students and faculty manage its wider impact, starting with transparency and consent. He uses "AI-awareness" for knowing how AI works, where students will meet it and what they need to make their own choices. His proposal is a pair of labels: assignment labels with simple icons that state what level of AI use is allowed, built with Claude, and a prototype consent label that tells both students and autonomous agents to stop and check whether a tool is covered by a campus data-protection licence before loading course materials. He admits the labels will not stop a determined student, and that models are trained to ignore hidden prompts, but says an explicit and standardised label is different from a hidden command and could one day be honoured like robots.txt. He surveys Stanford, Chicago and Penn State responses and Clay Shirky's call to redesign assessments, noting that these will take years while faculty can act this semester.
points: Frontier AI is moving faster than the public can follow, so students will look to professors for credible guidance on helpful versus harmful uses.
Many students use free commercial chatbots rather than the data-protected campus tools, and often upload instructors' materials without any thought to copyright or consent.
Per-assignment AI-use labels replace a policy statement students forget after week one and can also signal permitted help such as the writing centre.
A visible consent label aimed at both students and agents turns an upload into a moment of reflection on privacy and ownership.
He is candid that labels are not a cheat-proof barrier; the point is a transparent, standardised norm that developers could be pushed to honour.
quotes: Anthropic’s Fable 5.2 has arrived. It joins new releases from Google with Gemini 4 and last month’s release, OpenAI’s GPT-6.

Some people call their response AI-ready, AI literacy, or AI fluency. For our book, we choose AI-awareness. By AI-awareness, I mean recognizing how AI works, where students are likely to encounter it, and what they need to know to make their own choices about using it.
Within it, I asked Claude to code an updated guide to show my students how to turn off data tracking on the different AI tools they may encounter.

But in doing so, I began to wonder what might need to change about being transparent with instructions now that humans and bots are both in positions to read assignments. Both tools and humans need clear, explicit directions to function.

The labels alone won’t be 100% effective against all AI systems, and any such system should be cautious about suggesting otherwise. A determined student with some prompting skills will be able to bypass it, and a model might be programmed to ignore the added instructions.

Like the University of Chicago’s recent initiatives responding to AI, Stanford wants to balance their approach to “help departments determine when and how AI should be excluded from a course or major and identify what students should do without the aid of a chatbot.

These are all thoughtful responses, but they will each take years to realize. Faculty don’t have to wait. Talking with students about consent, copyright, and data protection, and labeling our materials so both students and bots get the message, is something we can start this semester.
